claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
First-principles searches for optimal multi-principal-element alloys have high computational demands.
CALPHAD predictions can become less accurate when binary and ternary thermodynamic parameters are extrapolated to high-entropy alloys.
CALPHAD does not directly calculate mechanical properties.
Machine-learning algorithms can predict mechanical properties of single-phase and multiphase alloys with reasonable accuracy.
A physics-informed surrogate using low-cost physical descriptors and machine-learning regression can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
Calibration on a limited set of targeted tensile and fracture experiments will improve the surrogate's predictive accuracy.
Misfit volumes, local elastic anisotropy, and interfacial-energy distributions encode the hierarchical heterostructure and localized chemical fluctuations.
The hierarchical heterostructure and localized chemical fluctuations mediate fracture and plasticity.
Combining inexpensive physical descriptors with machine learning can reduce reliance on large-scale DFT or CALPHAD calculations.
Effective elastic constants provide sufficient information for the surrogate to capture elastic response.
Descriptors linked to defects and local phase distributions enable prediction of inelastic and fracture behavior.
The surrogate will reduce computational demands by roughly one order of magnitude relative to previous high-fidelity methods.
The surrogate will reduce prediction errors for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness by approximately 15–20% relative to previous high-fidelity methods.
Traditional machine learning without integrated physical descriptors has limited reliability, particularly for toughness in hierarchical high-entropy alloys.
The approach should remain reliable for alloys sharing HfNbTiVAl10-like hierarchical microstructures and chemical-fluctuation scales under ambient-temperature tensile conditions.
Extensive phase transformations, strong temperature dependence, or markedly different microstructures may make the approach unreliable.
Fracture-toughness prediction is especially difficult because crack initiation and propagation are intrinsically multiscale.
The proposed benchmark measures Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness on multiple HfNbTiVAl10 batches under room-temperature inert-atmosphere conditions.
Prediction errors greater than 20% for any key property across a statistically significant number of samples would falsify predictive reliability.
